code.title: k8s-broken/README.md
code.src:
# Break-and-fix lab (Day 38)

A small online shop runs five services. Each one is broken in a different way.
Your job: find out why with `kubectl`, fix the YAML file, apply it again, and check the fix.

Do not open `SOLUTIONS.md` until you have tried each one. The skill you are practising is the
search, not the answer.

## Before you start

- Your kind cluster from Day 30 is running (`kubectl get nodes` shows three Ready nodes).
- The image is loaded into the cluster: `kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.0.0 --name devops`.
- Optional: metrics-server from Day 35, so `kubectl top` works.

## Start the lab

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-broken/
kubectl get pods -n debug-lab -w
```

Wait about two minutes before you start. Some problems only show after a few restarts.

## What the shop team reports

| Service | File | What people see |
|---|---|---|
| catalog | `01-catalog.yaml` | The Pod never starts. Its STATUS is `ErrImagePull`, then `ImagePullBackOff`. |
| checkout | `02-checkout.yaml` | The Pod stays `0/1` with STATUS `CreateContainerConfigError`. `kubectl logs` shows nothing. |
| search | `03-search.yaml` | Both Pods are `Running` and `1/1` Ready, but requests to `http://search.debug-lab` fail. |
| reports | `04-reports.yaml` | RESTARTS keeps going up. STATUS switches between `OOMKilled` and `CrashLoopBackOff`. |
| profile | `05-profile.yaml` | The Pod is `Running` and Ready, then restarts every half a minute or so. The logs look normal. |

To test the search service from inside the cluster, start a throwaway Pod:

```bash
kubectl run net-test -n debug-lab --rm -it --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://search
```

## The method (use it for every service)

1. `kubectl get pods -n debug-lab`: which Pod, which STATUS, how many RESTARTS.
2. `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n debug-lab`: read the Events at the bottom first, then `Last State`.
3. `kubectl logs <pod> -n debug-lab --previous`: what the crashed container printed before it died.
4. `kubectl get events -n debug-lab --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp`: everything that happened, in order.
5. For a Service: `kubectl get endpointslices -n debug-lab -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>`.
6. Compare what you found with the YAML file. Change one thing, `kubectl apply -f` the file, and watch again.

## You are done when

- `kubectl get pods -n debug-lab` shows every Pod `Running`, `1/1` Ready, and RESTARTS no longer going up for two minutes.
- The `net-test` command above prints JSON from the search service.

Clean up with `kubectl delete namespace debug-lab`.

Show a Pod's settings, Last State and Events; read the Events first.
Show what the crashed container printed before it died.

Show which Pod IPs a Service sends traffic to; `<unset>` means none.

Give that Role to the ServiceAccount viewer.

mistake: Deleting or restarting the broken Pod first, to see if it helps. A new Pod wipes the evidence you needed: the crashed container's logs, its Last State and often the newest Events. Run describe and `logs --previous` before you delete anything, and write down what you saw.
real_world: PayLite's on-call runbook starts with the same ladder: get, describe, logs `--previous`, events, endpoints. Most engineers have read-only RBAC in production, and the images are distroless, so `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container is the normal way to look inside. Fixes go through git and Argo CD; a `kubectl patch` in production is only for emergencies and is written up afterwards.

task.title: Break-and-fix: five broken services
steps: Check that `hello-devops:1.0.0` is loaded into kind and metrics-server is running. Copy the `k8s-broken/` folder into your repo.
Apply the whole folder with `kubectl apply -f k8s-broken/` and watch `kubectl get pods -n debug-lab -w` for two minutes. Note each Pod's STATUS and RESTARTS.

For each of the five services, follow the method from the README: get, describe with the Events first, `logs --previous`, events. Write one sentence per service: the cause, and the line of output that proves it.
For search, show that the Service has no endpoints, and compare its selector with the Pods' labels.
For reports, use `kubectl top pods` on a healthy hello-devops Pod to choose a sensible memory limit.
Fix one file at a time, apply it, and wait until that Pod is healthy before you move to the next.
Prove that search works with the `net-test` busybox command from the README.

RBAC: create a ServiceAccount `viewer` in `debug-lab`, a Role that may only get, list and watch Pods, and a RoleBinding. Check with `kubectl auth can-i` that it may list Pods but not delete them, then trigger the Forbidden error with `--as`.
Compare your notes with `SOLUTIONS.md` in the lab folder, then delete the `debug-lab` namespace.
hints: If `kubectl logs` shows nothing, ask whether the container ever started. If it never did, the answer is in the Events.
`kubectl get pod <pod> -n debug-lab -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}'` prints the last crash on one line.
For RBAC you need three commands: `kubectl create serviceaccount`, `kubectl create role` and `kubectl create rolebinding`. The commands list has the last two.
task.done_when: All five Pods in `debug-lab` are Running and 1/1 Ready with no new restarts, `net-test` gets JSON from search, and `kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n debug-lab --as=system:serviceaccount:debug-lab:viewer` says no.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how you would find out why a Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Mention which commands you run, in which order, and what each one can tell you.
explain_back.answer: First `kubectl get pods` to see the status and how many restarts there have been. Then `kubectl describe pod` and read the Events and `Last State`: the exit code tells me whether it was the app's own error, an OOM kill (137) or a failed liveness probe. Then `kubectl logs --previous`, because the current container may have printed nothing yet, while the crashed one has the error. If that is still not enough, I compare the config the Pod got, such as env vars, ConfigMaps and probes, with what the app expects.

recap: Debug bottom-up: Pod, then Service, then route, then node. Change one thing at a time.
Pending, ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff and CreateContainerConfigError: no logs yet, read the Events.
CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom; `logs --previous` and the exit code in Last State show the cause.
Healthy Pods but a failing Service usually means a selector or targetPort mismatch: check EndpointSlices.
`kubectl debug` adds an ephemeral container with tools; a throwaway busybox Pod checks DNS.
Forbidden is RBAC, not a bug: read the message, ask `kubectl auth can-i`, grant the smallest Role.

check.q: A new Pod stays Pending. Its event says `0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient memory`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the Pod's memory limit
Remove the taint from every node
Lower the memory request, or free up room
Add a readiness probe to the Pod
check.why: The two workers lack free memory for the request, and scheduling uses requests, so the request must shrink or room must appear.

check.q: A Pod shows `CreateContainerConfigError` and `kubectl logs` prints nothing. Why are the logs empty?
options: The container never started, so there is nothing to log; the Events explain why
The logs were deleted when the Pod restarted
The app writes logs to a file instead of standard output
kubectl needs `--previous` for every Pod with an error
check.why: The kubelet could not build the container's settings, usually because a ConfigMap or Secret is missing, so no process ever ran.

check.q: A CI job's ServiceAccount `deployer` in namespace `ci` gets Forbidden when it applies a Deployment to namespace `shop`. Which command checks the permission directly?
options: Read the Deployment's events in `shop`
Read the CI job's logs once more
Restart the CI runner and try again
Run `kubectl auth can-i` as that ServiceAccount
check.why: `kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer` asks the API server about that exact subject, action and namespace.

interview.q: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through how you debug it.
interview.a: I start with `kubectl get pods` for the restart count, then `kubectl describe pod` for the Events and the Last State with its exit code. Exit code 137 with OOMKilled points at memory, and a failed liveness probe shows up in the Events. A small code such as 1 means the app exited with its own error. Then `kubectl logs --previous` shows what the crashed container printed. If the image has no tools, I use `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container to check config, DNS or files from inside the Pod.

interview.q: The Pods are healthy, but requests to the Service fail. What do you check?
interview.a: First the Service's endpoints with `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>`; empty endpoints mean the selector matches no ready Pods. Then I compare the selector with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`, and check that `targetPort` matches the container's port. Next I test from inside the cluster with a throwaway busybox Pod, using the Service's DNS name, to rule out DNS. If all of that works, I look at NetworkPolicies and then at the Gateway or Ingress route in front of the Service.

interview.q: What is RBAC in Kubernetes, and how do you debug a Forbidden error?
interview.a: RBAC is role-based access control: Roles and ClusterRoles list allowed verbs on resources, and bindings give them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts. Permissions only add up; there are no deny rules. The Forbidden message names the subject, verb, resource and namespace, and `kubectl auth can-i` with `--as` confirms it. Then I add the smallest Role and RoleBinding that allow exactly that action, rather than a broad ClusterRole.

deeper.body:
Five more failures you will meet sooner or later, each with its first check:
- `exec format error` in the logs, right at start: the image was built for another CPU. On an Apple Silicon Mac, an image built only for amd64 cannot run on arm64 kind nodes. Build multi-platform images (Part 3) or pick an image that has an arm64 variant.
- `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` or `Init:0/1` for a long time: an init container fails or waits. Its logs need `-c <init-container-name>`.
- `Terminating` that never ends: something holds the object, often a finalizer waiting for a controller that is gone. `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'` shows it. Do not force-delete before you know what the finalizer protects.
- `Evicted` or `ContainerStatusUnknown` Pods left behind: the node ran short of memory or disk and evicted them (Day 35). The Deployment already replaced them; read the eviction message, then delete the leftovers.
- `Unable to connect to the server` from kubectl itself: the cluster is down or you are on the wrong context. `kubectl config current-context` should say `kind-devops`, and `docker ps` should show the kind node containers.

When the problem looks like the network, check in order: the name, the endpoints, the port, and then policy. A NetworkPolicy (Day 33) that selects a Pod blocks all traffic its rules do not allow. If `nslookup` works and the endpoints are there but connections time out, look for a policy with `kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>`.

At work, two more habits help. Write each incident down: the symptom, the command that showed the cause, the fix. After a few months that file is your team's best runbook. And automate the boring part: the `kubectl events --types=Warning` view and a few saved k9s shortcuts often find the problem before anyone opens a dashboard.

Finally, know where Kubernetes' own logs live. On kind, `docker exec devops-control-plane crictl ps` lists the control plane containers, and `kind export logs` collects logs from every node into a folder for you to read or attach to a bug report.
